writing.exampleCaption: The name says what must be true before work starts.
writing.explanation:
A condition is not an arbitrary number or string in Rust. Comparisons such as builds > 0 and errors == 0 each produce a bool. The example combines them into ready, a name that expresses the decision the program needs to make. That makes the if branch easy to inspect: it runs only after at least one build exists and no errors remain. If your code says if count, rustc asks for a real boolean condition instead of guessing whether zero should mean false.

The logical operators also control which work is performed. For left && right, a false left side settles the answer, so right is not evaluated. For left || right, a true left side settles it. This is short-circuiting, shown in the diagram by the crossed-out right branch. It matters when the right expression is expensive or valid only after the left has checked a precondition. Do not use side effects on the right merely because you expect them to run: the operator may skip them. Predict the result for each pair of boolean values, then use ! to reverse one condition and check that the branch still says what you intend.

You can use short-circuiting as a safe guard, for example checking that an index is in range before reading an element on the right side of &&. Reverse the order and the protection disappears. Parentheses help when a condition mixes && and ||: write the grouping you mean instead of making a future reader remember precedence. A descriptive name such as ready often makes the decision clearer than repeating the whole expression at every if.

writing.success: The branch runs only for the intended combination of values. You can explain why each skipped right-hand expression was unnecessary.
writing.summary: A comparison produces a bool, and a branch requires one. && and || can skip their right-hand expression as soon as the result is known.
writing.task: Build a clearly named condition from two comparisons. Predict whether the right side of && runs when the left is false, and whether the right side of || runs when the left is true.

illustration.alt: A comparison produces a bool; false skips the right side of &&, while true skips the right side of ||.
illustration.caption: Short-circuit operators evaluate only the right-hand expression needed to determine the result.
